CREATIVE AGENCY: Our sister studio focuses on inventing and interpreting brands — from established global organizations to independent start-ups — across a multitude of industries, including hospitality, residential, mixed-use, and retail. CUSTOM FURNITURE AND LIGHTING PRODUCTION: In concert with our trusted network of manufacturers, this company builds AvroKO Design’s uniquely detailed pieces that bring a one-of-a-kind signature to a project, while ensuring proper craftmanship and quality control. Goodshop also represents and produces AvroKO’s prolific portfolio of custom furniture and lighting for projects around the globe.

HOSPITALITY STRATEGY AND CONCEPT: AHG works with some of the world’s most visionary restaurateurs, chefs, mixologists, sommeliers, brands, hotel and resort operators, and real estate developers to provide a range of hospitality services, including Strategy & Planning, F&B Concept, Operational Development & Management, and Marketing/Programming Strategy & Implementation.

Aedas’ Nansha IFC with curved glass towers, sky garden connection and wave‑inspired façade overlooking the waterfront. Street‑level waterfront view of Aedas‑designed Nansha IFC in Guangzhou, showing two tall office towers with curved, slanted glass curtain walls rising from a sculpted podium. The façades feature undulating horizontal patterns and tilted glazing panels, while a sky garden links the twin towers above, framing landscaped forecourts and coastal public space below.

Aedas’ Yohoo Museum, Hangzhou—double-ring glazed art museum on a lake island with pedestrian bridges. Aerial view of Aedas’ Yohoo Museum in Hangzhou: interlocking double-ring steel-frame volume wrapped in glazed curtain wall with vertical/horizontal framing. Two oculus courtyards pierce the undulating roof. Building sits on a lake island with promenade, planted terraces and pedestrian bridges—useful for daylighting strategy, flood-resilient waterfront design and parametric façade analysis.

Aedas’ SLS Dubai Hotel & Residences—high-rise mixed-use tower with stepped façade, projecting balconies and curtain wall. Daytime exterior view of Aedas’ SLS Dubai Hotel & Residences: a slender mixed-use tower with a stepped massing profile, projecting balcony slabs and a glazed curtain-wall system. Vertical fins and deep balcony setbacks articulate the façade. Ground-level public realm shows pedestrian use typical of high-density, hot-arid urban environments.

Aedas’ Shenzhen T33 Tower—office complex with glass curtain wall, illuminated sky-terrace boxes and street frontage. Street-level dusk view of Aedas’ Shenzhen T33 Tower (Liuxiandong Headquarters Base): steel-frame office tower with glass curtain wall and three irregular cantilevered ‘cloud box’ terraces. Ground plane shows pedestrian edge and scooter parking. Façade lighting and floor-to-ceiling glazing support daylighting strategy, digital workplace design and urban ecology integration on site.

Aedas’ West Kowloon high‑speed rail station entrance with curved steel canopy and glazed transport concourse. Street‑level view of Aedas’ large‑span transport hub entrance featuring a curved steel roof canopy, inclined glass curtain wall, exposed structural ribs and integrated stair access. The concourse façade uses floor‑to‑ceiling glazing framed by metal panels, connecting the station interior with landscaped public realm in a dense urban setting.

Aedas’ Heartland 66 mixed‑use development with curved retail podium and high‑rise towers in Wuhan’s CBD. Street‑level view of Aedas’ Heartland 66 showing a curvilinear retail podium with a diamond‑pattern metal façade beneath adjacent high‑rise towers. The podium integrates recessed glazing at ground level and stepped terraces above. Pedestrian hardscape and public forecourt activate the streetscape within Wuhan’s dense, transit‑served urban environment.

Aedas’ Hengqin CRCC Plaza in Zhuhai is shown as a dynamic office complex formed by four crystalline towers linked by a sculptural sky bridge. The image highlights vertically ribbed glass façades wrapped with flowing metallic bands, creating a continuous “loop in the sky.” Integrated greenery, roof gardens, and a layered podium activate the public realm, establishing a distinctive business landmark within the emerging central business district.

Aedas’ Rixos Financial Centre Road Dubai Residences - supertall mixed-use tower with stepped crown and unitised glass façade in a high-density urban skyline. Aerial dusk view of an Aedas-designed supertall tower with a slender vertical profile, stepped upper volumes and continuous glass curtain wall. The building rises from a podium block within a dense city grid, surrounded by high-rise buildings and arterial roads, indicating integration with metropolitan infrastructure.

Aedas’ Capella Diriyah—low-rise luxury hotel with earth-toned masonry, fortress walls, palm-lined courtyards in desert setting. Aerial dusk view of Aedas’ Capella Diriyah in Saudi Arabia: low-rise hospitality complex formed by thick earth-toned masonry walls, corner towers and courtyards. Palm-lined landscape and perimeter walls define shaded circulation and arrival. The composition supports analysis of courtyard-based passive cooling, climate-responsive desert architecture and heritage-led luxury resort planning.

Aedas’ The Oberoi Wadi Safar—low-rise luxury resort with courtyard villas, palm groves and central water axis in desert terrain. Aerial dusk view of Aedas’ The Oberoi Wadi Safar in Saudi Arabia: low-rise resort villas organised along a linear water axis, framed by palm groves and courtyards. Earth-toned masonry volumes sit within desert topography, forming shaded pedestrian paths. Visible planning supports courtyard-based passive cooling, climate-responsive resort design and landscape-integrated luxury hospitality.

Aedas’ The Star in Singapore with elevated auditorium, open‑air retail podium and climate‑responsive structural canopy. Interior plaza view of Aedas‑designed The Star in Singapore, showing a vast open‑air atrium beneath an elevated auditorium supported by inclined concrete columns. Retail floors, escalators and staircases wrap the central void, while a high‑performance glazed façade and overhead roof structure modulate daylight and airflow within the public space.

Aedas’ Vida Dubai Mall twin towers above a stepped podium, framing a public lawn in Downtown Dubai. Twilight view of a public lawn in Downtown Dubai facing Aedas‑designed Vida Dubai Mall. Two slender high‑rise towers rise behind a stepped podium edge, with tower façades expressed by vertical glazing bands. The foreground shows an active public realm with seated visitors and open sightlines toward the skyline.

We're not here to greenwash—we're here to design spaces that last.

For us, sustainability isn't about chasing certifications or buzzwords. It's about making choices that respect materials, reduce waste, and create spaces people don't want to replace. That means adaptive reuse and renovations over demolition. Durable finishes over trendy ones. Quality pieces that can move with you, grow with you, and be repaired when needed.

We also believe plants and landscape aren't just aesthetic—they're essential to the human experience. Natural light, borrowed views, greenery, and fresh air aren't luxuries. They're what make a space feel good to inhabit.

The most sustainable choice is often the simplest: keep things out of the landfill. Buy once, buy well. Repair instead of replace. Design for longevity, not obsolescence.

Cheap materials don't save money when you're replacing and repairing constantly—they just fill landfills and create more work down the line. We'd rather invest in something that lasts.

Happy Earth Day. Here's to building better, not just more. 🌱

Apartment No. 201 started as a fragmented three-bedroom layout in Nicosia, Cyprus. Cypriot studio Anastasiou Misseri gave up one bedroom entirely, folding it into a walk-in wardrobe for the primary suite and bringing the apartment down to 99.40 sqm (1,070 sq ft) of continuous space.  A single run of joinery carries the kitchen cabinetry straight into the living room as display shelving, tying the rooms together in wood veneer, colored lacquer and marble. "We value craft and care in the process of building," the architects say. An 84-square-meter café and flower shop in Beijing's Haidian Park is built from thin, standard timber slats — chosen because the park's footpaths couldn't carry the machinery a heavier structure would need. The irregular footprint follows the gaps between existing trees rather than clearing them, and the bundled columns bend outward to carry a wide, woven canopy that reads, without ever aiming to, like a mushroom rising out of the grove.  Circular skylights set into the canopy let daylight fall in patches, custom shelves sized to the columns' threaded rods display the flowers, and a planted roof in cold-hardy species keeps its color through the winter months when the rest of the park has gone dormant. Bar Blondie's 200-bin wine list runs on four imagined creative figures rather than grape or region: The Director, built around Sergio Leone's cinema; The Architect, after Ray Eames; The Writer, after Joan Didion; and The Actor, reserved for emerging low-intervention producers.  Nottingham-based Macaulay Sinclair designed the interior of these converted early 20th-century horse stables as a mid-century artist's living room, mixing bespoke joinery with found pieces and art curated with The Art Office's Ryan Stanier. No load-bearing walls on the two main floors of Chalet Moraine, a 2025 lake house in Quebec's Laurentians. Contractor Gestion Séquence named their absence among the project's hardest challenges, saying the streamlined result took extensive calculation.  Montreal-based Appareil Architecture set the interior's service rooms free of the structure entirely, as freestanding volumes modeled on the glacial erratic boulders scattered through the surrounding forest. The ouroboros is a serpent devouring its own tail, a closed circle. Plastique Fantastique opened it. Commissioned by Bvlgari @bvlgari for its Serpenti Infinito series, auruBOROS rises from The Standard Hotel and uncoils along New York's High Line: 30 meters (98 feet) of golden mirrored TPU, inflated by ventilators.  The title fuses aurum, Latin for gold, with ouroboros. The gold is only a reflective skin. It returns fragments of brick, sky and the strangers standing next to you, and once the air stops, the serpent is gone. On view through September 20.
